title: Journalist reports Trump adviser discussed faithless electors after election loss
description_medium: On November 12, 2020, journalist Laurie Garrett reported that an unnamed Trump adviser said the campaign was working to persuade electors in 20 states to become “faithless electors” and vote for Donald Trump. The report came after Joe Biden had been projected the winner and before the Electoral College met. The source does not identify the adviser or document state commitments, so the reported claim should not be described as a confirmed coordinated plan.
description_long: After Joe Biden was projected to have won the 2020 presidential election, attention turned to the Electoral College and whether any electors might disregard their states’ popular vote results. On November 12, journalist Laurie Garrett wrote that a Trump adviser had told her that efforts were underway to persuade electors in 20 states to vote for Donald Trump instead. Such electors are commonly called “faithless electors.” The claim described an effort to alter the electoral outcome between the election and the Electoral College vote scheduled for December 14. Garrett’s report did not name the adviser or provide records showing that state electors had agreed to participate. The statement therefore documents a reported claim by an anonymous source, rather than proof that twenty state delegations or officials had committed to a plan. Biden’s electoral victory was confirmed when electors met and cast their votes. The controversy illustrates the period’s efforts to challenge the result, while the precise identity and role of the adviser in Garrett’s report remain unknown.
evidence_notes: Laurie Garrett’s November 12, 2020 post is the source for the anonymous adviser’s claim. It is not corroboration of a 20-state plan; the public record shows the electors voted December 14 for Biden and Trump. National Archives documents the Electoral College result.
corrected_wording: Attributed the 20-state assertion to Garrett’s unnamed source and avoided presenting an unverified plan as fact.
exact_blocker: The adviser’s identity, the states allegedly involved, and any actual commitments or organizing steps cannot be established from the cited report.

title: Trump administration’s zero-tolerance policy separates migrant families
description_medium: In spring 2018, the Trump administration’s zero-tolerance policy led federal officials to prosecute adults crossing the border without authorization, while children were placed separately in government custody. The policy caused large numbers of parent-child separations, and agencies were not prepared to track and care for the separated children. A federal judge ordered the government to reunite eligible families in June 2018. Later reviews documented serious failures in identification, communication, and reunification.
description_long: In spring 2018, the Trump administration adopted a “zero-tolerance” approach that referred adults who crossed the U.S.-Mexico border without authorization for criminal prosecution. When parents were transferred for prosecution, children were treated as unaccompanied minors and placed in the custody of the Department of Health and Human Services. The policy produced large numbers of family separations, including cases involving young children, and federal agencies had not developed a system to track all families or prepare for the scale of the change. In June 2018, a federal court ordered the government to reunite families covered by the case, and later oversight reports described difficulty identifying parents and coordinating care. The HHS inspector general found that limited planning and poor communication impeded the department’s response, while the Government Accountability Office reported that agencies had not planned for the increase in separated children. These records document an enforcement policy that separated families and left agencies struggling to provide care and reunite children with their parents.
evidence_notes: GAO and HHS OIG establish policy context, separations, lack of planning, and reunification difficulties. Omit unsupported absolute counts and intent/legal conclusions such as torture.
corrected_wording: Replaced fabricated torture/racketeering-style assertions with the documented policy, separations, oversight findings, and court-ordered reunification context.

title: Reports say Netanyahu met Pompeo and Saudi crown prince in Neom
description_medium: Israeli media and an Israeli government source reported that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secretly traveled to Neom, Saudi Arabia, on November 22, 2020, to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo. Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister denied that Netanyahu attended, saying only Saudi and U.S. officials were present. Pompeo confirmed his Saudi meetings but Washington did not confirm the reported trilateral meeting. The report fueled speculation about possible Israel-Saudi normalization.
description_long: On November 22, 2020, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in the Saudi city of Neom during a regional tour. Israeli media then reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad chief Yossi Cohen had also traveled there for a meeting with the crown prince and Pompeo. An Israeli government source confirmed the visit to Reuters, and an Israeli cabinet minister publicly referred to the meeting. Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan denied that Netanyahu had met the crown prince, saying that he had met Pompeo at the airport and that only Saudi and U.S. officials were present. The State Department did not confirm a three-way meeting. The conflicting accounts made the reported encounter a subject of international attention because Saudi Arabia and Israel had no formal diplomatic relations and the Trump administration was pressing for regional normalization agreements. The meeting should therefore be described as reported by Israeli sources and denied by Riyadh; its agenda and any decisions were not publicly established.
evidence_notes: Reuters and WaPo reported Israeli media and source confirmation; Saudi Foreign Minister explicitly denied Netanyahu’s presence. Pompeo’s trip and MBS meeting were public; agenda or agreement is not established.
corrected_wording: Attributed the secret Netanyahu meeting to Israeli reports and included Saudi Arabia’s denial; did not state an undisclosed outcome.

title: Lawyers receive new contact data to locate parents separated from migrant children
description_medium: On December 2, 2020, lawyers working to reunite families separated at the U.S.-Mexico border said the Justice Department had provided additional phone numbers and addresses that could help them find parents. A court filing said the whereabouts of 628 parents remained unknown at that point. The effort followed separations under the Trump administration’s zero-tolerance policy and a federal court order requiring reunification of eligible families.
description_long: Lawyers overseeing court-ordered reunification efforts said on December 2, 2020, that the federal government had provided new contact information for families separated at the U.S.-Mexico border. The data included phone numbers and addresses that had not previously been known to the lawyers. The disclosure came after repeated requests for information and as the government reported that the whereabouts of 628 parents remained unknown. The number referred to parents of children affected by the separations, not to a final count of every child who had been separated. The reunification effort began after a federal judge ordered the government to identify and reunite families separated under the Trump administration’s border policy. Lawyers and nonprofit organizations were coordinating searches, contacting relatives, and trying to locate parents who had been deported or released elsewhere. The additional records offered new leads, but locating families remained difficult because government agencies had not maintained a complete tracking system. The episode showed how delayed access to contact information affected the practical work of finding separated families years after the policy began.
evidence_notes: NBC report as cited in the input and contemporaneous UPI/AP coverage describe additional contact information and 628 parents still unlocated. Oversight report documents the deficient tracking system.
corrected_wording: Replaced “caught hiding” with the documented report of new contact data and ongoing court-supervised searches.

title: Trump indicted over classified documents kept at Mar-a-Lago; case later dismissed
description_medium: After leaving office, Donald Trump retained boxes of government records at Mar-a-Lago, including documents marked classified. The National Archives retrieved 15 boxes in January 2022; after investigators sought additional records and the FBI searched the property in August, a federal grand jury indicted Trump on charges including willful retention of national defense information and obstruction. Trump denied wrongdoing. In July 2024, the judge dismissed the case, ruling that the special counsel was unlawfully appointed; prosecutors dropped the appeal against Trump after his 2024 election victory.
description_long: When Donald Trump left the White House in January 2021, boxes of presidential records went with him to Mar-a-Lago in Florida. The National Archives retrieved 15 boxes in January 2022 and later notified the Justice Department that they contained classified materials. After a grand jury subpoena sought further documents and investigators concluded that records remained at the property, the FBI executed a search warrant there on August 8, 2022. In June 2023, a federal grand jury indicted Trump and aide Walt Nauta. The indictment alleged that Trump willfully retained national-defense information and conspired to obstruct efforts to recover it; Trump pleaded not guilty and denied wrongdoing. In July 2024, U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon dismissed the case, finding that Special Counsel Jack Smith’s appointment violated the Appointments Clause. Prosecutors appealed, but after Trump won the 2024 election, the Justice Department asked the appeals court to dismiss the case against him, citing its policy against prosecuting a sitting president. The case ended without a trial or verdict on the underlying allegations.
evidence_notes: The indictment states allegations, not proven guilt. NARA confirms receipt of 15 boxes. Judge Cannon’s dismissal rested on the appointment issue; the appeal was later dismissed at DOJ’s request after Trump’s election.
corrected_wording: Reframed sensational “theft/betrayal” language as a factual timeline of record recovery, indictment allegations, denial, dismissal, and absence of a merits trial.

title: Trump pressures Justice Department to support his 2020 election claims
description_medium: After Attorney General William Barr resigned in December 2020, President Donald Trump repeatedly pressed Acting Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen and Deputy Richard Donoghue to investigate alleged election fraud and publicly support his claims. A Justice Department official, Jeffrey Clark, drafted a letter asserting that the department had identified concerns in Georgia and urging state officials to reconsider the election. Rosen and senior officials refused to send it. Trump considered replacing Rosen with Clark, but abandoned the plan after department and White House lawyers warned they would resign.
description_long: In the weeks after the 2020 election, President Donald Trump sought to use the Justice Department to advance his claims that the vote had been stolen. After Attorney General William Barr announced his resignation, Trump repeatedly contacted Acting Attorney General Jeffrey Rosen and acting deputy Richard Donoghue, asking them to investigate alleged fraud and declare the election corrupt. Jeffrey Clark, an assistant attorney general, drafted a letter to Georgia officials claiming the department had identified significant concerns and urging the state legislature to consider the appointment of electors. Rosen and Donoghue rejected the claims and would not send the letter. In early January 2021, Trump considered replacing Rosen with Clark. During an Oval Office meeting on January 3, Rosen, Donoghue, senior Justice Department officials, and White House counsel Pat Cipollone warned that a firing would prompt mass resignations. Trump ultimately did not replace Rosen, and the department did not issue Clark’s letter. The episode became a central example in congressional investigations of pressure on the Justice Department during the attempt to overturn the election result.
evidence_notes: Jan. 6 Committee report and contemporaneous oversight document releases describe Trump’s contacts, Clark’s proposed letter, and the January 3 meeting. Descriptions of a plan to “steal” the election are political characterization; the underlying documented actions are stated.
corrected_wording: Corrected headline and event title to describe pressure on DOJ; clarified Clark’s proposal was not issued and Rosen remained in place.

title: Trump promises to be “your retribution” in 2023 campaign speech
description_medium: At the Conservative Political Action Conference on March 4, 2023, former president and presidential candidate Donald Trump promised supporters that he would be their “warrior,” “justice,” and “retribution.” He framed the 2024 campaign around restoring what he called a country in decline and responding to perceived grievances. The phrase drew criticism and concern about how a future administration might treat political opponents, but the speech did not itself specify a federal law-enforcement program or named targets.
description_long: Donald Trump addressed the Conservative Political Action Conference in National Harbor, Maryland, on March 4, 2023, as he campaigned for the Republican presidential nomination. In the speech, he cast the 2024 election as a struggle over the direction of the country, attacked political opponents, and promised supporters, “I am your warrior, I am your justice, and for those who have been wronged and betrayed, I am your retribution.” The line became one of the speech’s most widely discussed moments. Trump’s language echoed themes of grievance and political payback that were central to his campaign messaging. It prompted debate about whether he would use presidential authority against people he viewed as opponents if returned to office. The remarks themselves were a campaign promise framed in broad terms; they did not name targets, lay out a plan for federal agencies, or establish that a government program of retaliation had been implemented. The speech’s broad language left supporters and critics to debate how he might translate the promise into governing decisions.
evidence_notes: CNN transcript and video document the March 4, 2023 CPAC speech and the retribution line. The provided Time link discusses vaccines and is unrelated to this event. Do not extend campaign rhetoric into a claim of enacted policy.
corrected_wording: Retained the documented quote while removing unsupported assertions about a comprehensive plan, targets, constitutional violations, or actual government persecution.

title: Trump urges Capitol rioters to go home while repeating false election claims
description_medium: After a mob of Trump supporters forced its way into the U.S. Capitol on January 6, 2021, Trump posted a video telling them to go home while repeating his false claim that the election had been stolen. At 6:01 p.m., as Guard troops arrived and police worked to secure the building, he tweeted that a “sacred landslide election victory” had been “stripped away” and again told the crowd to leave peacefully. Congress later resumed counting electoral votes.
description_long: On January 6, 2021, supporters of President Donald Trump stormed the U.S. Capitol as Congress met to count electoral votes. Lawmakers were evacuated, police officers were injured, and the joint session was suspended. At 4:17 p.m., Trump released a video telling the rioters to go home, but also repeating his false claim that the election had been stolen and saying, “We love you. You’re very special.” At 6:01 p.m., he posted another message describing the election as a “sacred landslide election victory” that had been “viciously stripped away,” again telling supporters to go home “with love & in peace.” National Guard reinforcements arrived at the Capitol around 5:40 p.m., and police worked through the evening to clear and secure the grounds. Congress reconvened later that night and completed the electoral vote count confirming Joe Biden’s victory. Trump’s statements came after hours of violence and continued to frame the attack through his false election claims.
evidence_notes: Jan. 6 Committee report documents Trump’s 4:17 video and 6:01 post; FactCheck.org provides troop-arrival sequence; Reuters covers Congress resuming its work. The original headline’s “Democrats earned the attack” was not supported by the record.
corrected_wording: Replaced the unsupported “earned the attack” assertion with Trump’s documented messages and context of the Capitol attack and response.
